summary: This best current practice formalizes an ad hoc practice of giving the IETF Nominating Committee advice about the operations of the IETF Administrative Oversight Committee. It updates RFC 7437 and was replaced by RFC 8713.

plainLanguage.summary: A committee choosing leaders gets a helper who explains how the business side of the organization works.

questions: what is the iaoc advisor to the nomcom
subtitle: Advising the Nominating Committee about IETF administration

tldr.problem: The IETF Nominating Committee selects leaders for the IETF but may lack expertise about how the IETF's administrative body operates, and there was no formal process to get this advice.
tldr.mechanism: This best current practice formalizes an existing informal practice by requiring that when the Nominating Committee is evaluating or could benefit from guidance on IETF administration, it should explicitly request an IAOC (IETF Administrative Oversight Committee) advisor to help it understand those operations.
tldr.outcome: The RFC updates RFC 7437 to make the role of IAOC advisor formal and documented, ensuring future Nominating Committees have access to this expertise. It was replaced by RFC 8713.

facts.label: Proposed by
facts.value: Nominating Committee request to IAOC or committee member proposal

today: RFC 8318 updates BCP 10 (RFC 7437) and is a Best Current Practice. It was replaced by RFC 8713, which superseded RFC 7437.

sections.title: The Nominating Committee and Administrative Oversight
sections.content:
The IETF Nominating Committee (NomCom) is responsible for selecting and confirming members of several IETF leadership bodies, including the IETF Administrative Oversight Committee (IAOC), which oversees the administrative structure and operations of the IETF itself.

In practice, the Nominating Committee members who are not specialists in IETF administration may lack detailed knowledge about how the IAOC operates, what its responsibilities are, and what expertise or experience is important for its members. Without this context, the committee may not be able to properly evaluate candidates or provide good oversight of the IAOC's work.

For many years, the IAOC has informally sent a representative to help answer questions from the Nominating Committee, but this practice was never officially documented in the process rules.
sections.plainLanguage: A committee picks new leaders for the business side of the organization. The committee members might not know how that side works, so someone from that side comes to explain it.

sections.title: From Informal Practice to Formal Role
sections.content:
RFC 7437 previously allowed any committee member to propose adding an advisor or liaison to the Nominating Committee, but it did not specifically encourage or document the practice of requesting IAOC expertise. Beginning around 2010, the IAOC informally provided a representative to each Nominating Committee.

However, in 2016, when the Nominating Committee was not selecting an IAOC member (because a mid-term vacancy had been filled by a longer-term appointment), the opportunity to request an IAOC advisor was overlooked—precisely because this practice was not part of the documented process. Similarly, in 2017, the practice was almost missed again.

This document formalizes the ad hoc practice so that future Nominating Committees will explicitly remember to request IAOC expertise. It also renames the role from 'liaison' to 'advisor' to better reflect what the person actually does and to avoid confusion with the more formal and demanding role of organizational liaison.
sections.plainLanguage: For years someone did this unofficially. But twice the committee almost forgot to ask. So they wrote it down to make sure it does not get forgotten.

sections.title: The Updated Process
sections.content:
RFC 8318 updates RFC 7437 by adding new text to Section 4.3 Structure. The change encourages committee members to propose an IAOC advisor and specifies that the Nominating Committee may choose to ask the IAOC to suggest someone knowledgeable about its operations, although the committee still votes to approve whoever is proposed.

The role is defined as an advisor rather than a liaison. An advisor is a non-voting participant whose duties are specified by the invitation that appointed them, in this case to help the committee understand IAOC operations. Unlike liaisons, advisors are not expected to monitor the committee's process, file disputes, or serve as backup chair candidates. This lighter designation prevents overloading the IAOC representative with responsibilities beyond answering questions about IAOC operations.

The document also makes clear that the advisor need not be a sitting IAOC member. This is important because many IAOC members are subject to review by the current Nominating Committee, which could create a conflict of interest. The IAOC has flexibility to send whoever it judges most qualified to explain its operations.
sections.plainLanguage: The updated rules say the committee should ask the business side to send an explainer. The explainer just answers questions; they do not have to watch the committee or be a boss.

sections.title: Why This Approach
sections.content:
The RFC includes a detailed appendix explaining why this solution was chosen over alternatives. Rather than create an entirely new IAOC-specific role (which would be complex and might become obsolete if the IAOC itself changed structure), the authors decided to reuse the existing "advisor" role from RFC 7437, which is simpler and has survived many Nominating Committee cycles.

The role is explicitly an "advisor" rather than a "liaison" because liaisons carry obligations from RFC 7437 that are not necessary for this purpose: liaisons must monitor the committee's execution, can be asked to resolve disputes, and are part of the pool of people eligible to become acting chair if needed. These responsibilities are too demanding for someone whose only job is to answer questions about IAOC operations.

Similarly, the IAOC is not required to send a sitting member. Some years, no sitting member might be available and willing, or the IAOC might judge that someone else in the community would be a better explainer. This flexibility allows the role to work reliably across many Nominating Committee cycles and organizational changes.
sections.plainLanguage: They chose the simplest approach that works: ask the business side to send someone smart who is not busy with other big jobs.
